1:
Who the fallen star is divides the commentators completely, and the disagreement is not about detail but about kind. Wesley makes it a good angel, belonging to the invisible world and quite different from the star of the previous chapter, so that the pit is opened by a holy messenger and the falling means only coming swiftly and with great force. Ellicott argues the opposite from the grammar and the parallels: the seer saw not a star falling but a star already fallen, an emblem used of Lucifer in Isaiah and by Christ of Satan as lightning, so that some great power or ruler is meant, and the eleventh verse — which gives the locusts a king — confirms that a diabolical agency is in view; to understand it of a good angel, he says, seems hardly possible. Robertson supports that reading from the tense alone, the perfect participle meaning already down, against the aorist used of the lightning-flash elsewhere and the present used of an angel coming up. Henry reports the historical identifications instead: some take the star for an eminent bishop and some for Boniface the third, who took the title of universal bishop by favour of an emperor who, being a usurper in the state, let him be one in the church as the reward of his flattery — after which, having ceased to be a minister of Christ, he became the devil's turnkey. Gill applies the whole to Mahomet and the publishing of the Alcoran. Clarke reports the field with visible impatience: some think the angel means Satan and the pit hell, some suppose Mohammed is meant, and one writer professes to believe that the German reformer is intended.

The smoke is read as doctrine by most and as physics by one. Bede takes the star for the old enemy who opened the heart of his own by blasphemous teaching, and the smoke for the madness of heresy, which labours to obscure not only the weak but the light of the lofty. Clarke glosses it simply as false doctrine obscuring the true light of heaven, and Gill as the decrees and articles of faith imposed on men's consciences. Wesley makes it the idolatrous doctrine of the Persians and its false zeal, breaking out in an uncommon paroxysm,. Ellicott alone attends to what kind of darkening this is: in the previous vision the light was obscured by the smiting of the luminaries themselves, here by a cause external to them, so that in the one the light-giving power was enfeebled and in the other the light is not enfeebled but hindered — a distinction, he insists, that must be remembered. Barnes explains the smoke from the contents of the pit, which he takes to be filled with burning sulphur after the manner of the lake in the later chapters, and probably drawn from the destruction of the cities of the plain.

The locusts are then identified as variously as the star. Gill rules out the literal insect, since these do not touch the grass and do have a king, and rules out devils and the Goths and Vandals as well, settling on the eastern and western antichrists. Clarke takes them for vast hordes of military troops, holding that the description agrees better with the Saracens than with any other nation though it may also fit the Romans, and suggests that the scorpions may signify archers. Wesley makes them the Persians and supplies a chronology to match, the academies stopped in one year, a president put to death, an insurrection lasting seven years. Ellicott holds the reference to the Egyptian plague and to Joel, where the locusts darken the land, and notes that these are armed instead with the power of scorpions, to sting and torture. Robertson agrees on the plague and calls them, after Swete, a swarm of hellish locusts.
4:
The limits laid on the locusts are given impersonally, and Barnes will not let that pass: the text does not say who issued the command, and though the most natural reading is that God gave it, he thinks it remarkable that this is not directly affirmed, and notes that the language would equally admit the king of the pit named a few verses later. What the restraint means is disputed along the old line between figure and history. Clarke gives two readings at once, that the grass and trees stand for the common people, the middling sort and the nobles, and that the sparing of them looks rather like the prudent counsel of a military chief who will need the crops for his own campaign. Barnes takes it as the mark that distinguishes these invaders from every other, that they carry the war against men and not against orchards and green fields. Robertson observes only that the vegetation had already been hurt sufficiently by the hail of the previous trumpet.

The exemption of the sealed is read as narrowly or as widely as each writer's scheme requires. Clarke identifies the unsealed as all false, hypocritical and heterodox Christians. Wesley makes them principally the unbelieving Israelites, adding that many who were called Christians suffered with them. Barnes hesitates between those who were not in reality the friends of God and those merely regarded as such. Ellicott draws a different conclusion from the same clause, that locusts sent not to injure vegetation and unable to touch the sealed are plainly not literal locusts; and he presses the promise of Luke 10:19 that nothing shall by any means hurt them, noting that it was given immediately after the saying about Satan falling as lightning, exactly as the safety of the sealed here follows the vision of the fallen star, a coincidence he thinks hardly undesigned. But he refuses to make the promise more than it is: no one has maintained that Christ promised freedom from danger, pain or death, only that no real injury can happen. Robertson reaches the same exemption by the older route, quoting Swete that as Israel in Egypt escaped the plagues that punished their neighbours, so the new Israel is exempted.

On the five months the two grammarians agree and Clarke divides. Ellicott takes them for the ordinary span of a locust plague and so, after Stuart, for a short period; Robertson says the same from natural history, the insect born in the spring and dead at the end of summer. Clarke offers a literal reckoning, either the May to September of the siege year, or the nearly five months that Cestius Gallus lay before Jerusalem, and then the alternative of prophetic months at a day for a year, which yields a hundred and fifty. Gill takes the ban on killing as a limit on conquest rather than on time: the Saracens ravaged the eastern empire and never destroyed it or took Constantinople, and the western locusts, the monks and friars, kill souls but not bodies.

The sting and the flight of death close the passage. Clarke suspects the scorpion here is the weapon of that name, a poisoned arrow, and produces Isidore's definition and Seneca's description of the burning it causes. Ellicott keeps to the creature and collects the parallels, the scorpions of Ezekiel 2:6, the bee summoned against Assyria, the psalmist's swarm, and calls such times reigns of terror. Barnes notices that the sufferers are not said to lay hands on themselves but only to look for death as a release, and thinks that circumstance of some importance as showing what kind of men they were. Robertson quotes Swete that physical death is no remedy for the torment of an evil conscience, and sets the passage against Paul's preference for departing, a very different feeling from this one.
7:
The description of the locusts sets off a hunt for anatomy, and one commentator refuses to join it. Barnes collects the travellers: Robinson's Bedouin called an insect of Sinai soldiers' horses; the editor of the Pictorial Bible says the comparison arose spontaneously on first seeing locusts browse with folded wings, before he had met the figure or recalled this text; the Italians call the insect a little horse; Cazvini divided locusts into horsemen and footmen; Niebuhr heard a Bedouin liken the head to a horse, the feet to a camel, the belly to a serpent, and dismissed it as Arab fancy until he heard it again at Bagdad. Ellicott rehearses the same reports and then declines the whole method: it seems to him doubtful whether in this or in any of these descriptions there is a reference to the anatomical features of the locust at all. He is at his driest on the faces, where the crown has been sought in the antennae and in the ridge of the thorax, and where it has actually been said that the locust bears under ordinary circumstances a distant resemblance to the human countenance — the adjective, he remarks, is most needful. Robertson takes the other side and reports that Vincent does see a distinct resemblance in the face, adding from Swete that human faces on demonic locusts suggest the intelligence and capacity of man.

The historical identifications run on as before. Clarke reads the whole as an overwhelming military force answering to the troops of Mohammed, the Arabs being such horsemen that horse and rider seem one animal, though he allows the Romans were eminent for cavalry too; the crowns are turbans and also the extent of the conquests; and the faces of men mean that though locusts in the symbol they are really men. Wesley makes them Persians, a people neither thoroughly civilised nor entirely savage, expert in horsemanship, wearing turbans for crowns and faces friendly and agreeable. Gill takes the hair for the Saracens, citing Pliny that the Arabians wore their hair long and uncut and were attired as women, and derives their names from women — Hagarenes from Hagar and Saracens from Sarah, unless from roots meaning to rob or to comb; then he turns it on the monks and friars, who dress more like women than men and claim the Virgin for patroness.

Whether the long hair carries any note of effeminacy is a real disagreement. Barnes thinks it struck John as remarkable precisely because warriors did not commonly wear it, and reads it as a mark of unusual appearance if not of softness. Robertson denies the whole suggestion on the grammar, since the faces are those of men in the generic sense and not of males, so that the hair is length and nothing else, and guesses at the antennae. Ellicott canvasses the hairy locust of Jeremiah 51:27, thinks the application uncertain, and offers the third stage of the insect, when the wings are still in rough horny cases. Clarke says only that no razor passes upon their flesh.

On the breastplates and the noise of wings all of them go to Joel 2, from which the teeth of lions and the chariots are drawn. Barnes takes the iron for the hard cuticle that shields the insect and cites Volney's description of Syrian locusts, noting that Volney had no intention of illustrating the truth of Scripture. Robertson observes that the scaly backs do resemble coats of mail, and quotes Swete that these locusts of the abyss may be the memories of the past brought home at times of divine visitation. Gill allegorises instead: the iron is hardness of heart and seared conscience, the protection of princes and laws made in their favour, breastplates not of righteousness and faith but worn against the truth, and the iron colour may be the black of their habit.
10:
Where the power of these creatures is lodged draws out both the grammarians. Robertson notes that the word for sting serves for the spur of a cock, the quill of the porcupine and the goad used on oxen, and that the vision deliberately puts the power to hurt in the tails, when it might have been placed in other organs. Barnes goes further and denies the insect any sting at all: the only thing resembling one is a hard bony needle with which the female pierces bark to lay her eggs, and it has no adaptation for conveying poison into a wound; he also separates the verb here, which means to do wrong or deal unjustly, from the word for torment in the earlier verse, and concludes that the distress is the distress of injustice rather than of bodily pain. Gill and Clarke read the tail as doctrine — the prophet who teaches lies being the tail — and name Mahomet and the Romish clergy. On the five months Clarke and Wesley apply the same day-for-a-year rule and reach different totals, Clarke a hundred and fifty years and Wesley seventy-nine; Wesley also insists that each tail is like a scorpion, not like the tail of a scorpion.

Ellicott stops the search itself. It is utterly vain, he says, to look for features of the ordinary locust answering to these particulars,. Most of the visions of this book, he adds, cannot be pictorially realised without incongruities that would be grotesque and profane, since principles and truths are the writer's main concern; the exigencies of the symbolism are quite beyond any natural insect.

The king is where the contrast is sharpest. Ellicott and Robertson both fix on Proverbs 30:27, that the locust has no king: real swarms march with wonderful precision and no presiding monarch, so the controlling head here marks the movement as no undesigned instinct but the offspring of a hidden spiritual force — the invasions and tyrannies that trouble mankind being tokens of a conflict between the spirit of destruction and the spirit of salvation. Ellicott takes Abaddon as the place of destruction in Job 26:6 and refuses to seek a great historical personage for the fulfilment at all. Robertson traces the word to the Wisdom books, notes its personification in the Talmud, leaves open whether Apollyon means Death or Satan, and reports Bousset's suggestion of an indirect allusion to Apollo, one of whose symbols was the locust, calling it a doubtful point assuredly. Wesley distinguishes Abaddon from the dragon, whose proper name is Satan. Barnes allows either that the evil angel commanded the hosts personally or that his spirit was infused into their leader; Clarke reports that some think Mohammed and some Vespasian; Gill makes him Mahomet outright, king of the eastern locusts as the pope is of the western.

The application is then argued at length and by dates. Barnes builds the case for Mohammed out of Gibbon, whose Mohammed was commanded to propagate his religion by the sword and told his followers that the sword is the key of heaven and hell and that a drop of blood shed in the cause of God avails more than two months of fasting and prayer — and Barnes takes the commission against the unsealed to mean the war waged on idolaters. Wesley dates the close of the first woe to 589, when the Persian power was broken and Mahomet was twenty, and follows the second through Chosroes and through the usurper Phocas, who in 606 made the bishop of Rome universal bishop. Ellicott, opening the sixth trumpet, says the aim of the plague is to exhibit the death-working power of false thoughts and false worships, and that such evils are to a great extent the creation of those who suffer them.
13:
The voice comes from the horns of the golden altar, and each writer takes something different from that. Barnes reconstructs the furniture — the altar of acacia overlaid with gold its four projecting horns of Exodus 30:2 which he thinks were mainly ornamental — and observes that the image is transferred to heaven, so that the order seems to issue from the very place where offerings are made to God. Wesley draws the sharper inference: this is the heavenly pattern of the altar of incense, and a voice from it signifies that the wrath now to be executed shall at no intercession be delayed any longer. Clarke takes the mention as evidence of another kind altogether, calling it a not very obscure indication that the Jewish temple was still standing when this was written.

Who the four bound angels are is disputed, and so is what kind of beings they are. Wesley reasons from their captivity that they must be evil, since they would not otherwise have been bound, and admits that why or how long they were bound we do not know. Robertson instead makes them the leaders of the demonic horsemen and holds that both quaternions in the book are agents of God's wrath. Barnes will not insist that angels were literally employed, though he grants that nobody can demonstrate the contrary, and doubts whether the number four means four divisions of anything rather than simply a great force. Clarke reports the guesses — Arabs, Saracens, Tartars, Turks, or else the four generals of Vespasian posted in Arabia, Africa, Alexandria and Palestine. Henry and Gill agree on the Turkish power: Henry notes that the instruments of God's anger may lie at a great distance from those they will punish, the Euphrates being far from the European nations, and that the enemies of the church are restrained until God gives the word; Gill dates the passage of the river and the founding of the Ottoman empire to about 1301. Robertson supplies the river itself, the eastern boundary of the Roman empire next to Parthia.

The hour and day and month and year divide the commentators three ways, and the division is about method as much as arithmetic. Wesley calculates: the components resolve into two hundred and twelve years, which he matches to the long slaughter made by the Saracens after Mahomet's death, and he finds the number of the angels answered by the number of the first and most eminent caliphs, Ali, Abubeker, Omar and Osman. Clarke sets out the same components — twenty-four hours to a day, four weeks to a month, twelve months to a year — and then refuses the sum, thinking that probably no more is meant than that these angels were at all times prepared and permitted,, remarking that those who understand the divisions as prophetic periods he must simply refer elsewhere, not professing to discuss such uncertainties. Ellicott denies the premise that both share. The English version reads as though the four measures gave the length of the plague, and the historical school has spent great ingenuity finding a period to match; but the phrase means made ready unto the hour, not lasting for it, and so marks a definite appointed moment whose year and month and day are known, much as our Lord spoke of the day and hour that no man knows. What it teaches, he says, is that there is a certain though unknown moment when the latent powers of retribution wake, and men who cry peace where there is no peace are dwelling meanwhile in a house built on sand. Barnes keeps to duration but reports Stuart on the other side, and Henry, who takes it as duration too, adds that prophetic characters of time are hardly to be understood by us. Robertson says only that all preparation is over and the angels wait for the signal.
16:
The number is two myriads of myriads, and nobody quite knows what to do with it. Barnes converts it to two hundred millions, allows that no such army was ever assembled, and guesses that the phrasing preserves something of how they were counted, squadrons reckonable by ten thousands and too many to number. Clarke agrees on the arithmetic and adds that such a host could not find forage in any part of the earth, so that perhaps only multitudes without number are meant; then he turns on the school that will have its system supported out of this most obscure book and tells us the figure covers every soldier employed in the war from beginning to end — those who can receive this saying, he says, let them receive it. Ellicott hears an echo of Psalm 68:17 and thinks the bewildering size of the number might have been enough by itself to keep interpreters from looking for a slavishly literal fulfilment. Robertson notes only that the word is the term for cavalry as against infantry. Gill reads the number as proof that the four angels were men, and finds the Turks in it, whose armies were chiefly horse, who kept twice as many mounts as men, and before whose generals a horse's tail is still carried as an ensign.

The three colours of the breastplates are given four different values. Barnes takes fire to mean simply red, burnished and blazing, and jacinth to be the deep purple or reddish blue of the flower. Clarke reads them flatly as red, blue and yellow. Ellicott matches the three hues to the threefold stream from the mouths and identifies jacinth as the dark purple often seen in smoke, quoting the Laureate's azure pillars of the hearth and remarking that this smoke is darker, being generated among death-giving elements. Robertson says the word means a red bordering on black, and observes that the Greek has no particle of comparison here at all, the three adjectives being metaphors outright.

Clarke then asks the question that governs the passage for two of these writers: is this an allegorical description of great ordnance? Cannons, he suggests, with horses' heads formed on their muzzles, fire and smoke and brimstone standing well for gunpowder, and the Ottomans made great use of heavy artillery against the Greeks of the lower empire; the power in the tails is the breech where the charge is lodged, and brass ordnance is often ornamented at muzzle and breech alike. Gill does not ask, he assumes: the power in their mouth is in their guns and what came out of them, and Constantinople was taken in this way, with which the empire ceased. He adds a textual note, that several versions and the Complutensian read by these three plagues, and that where the earlier chapter made the western empire the third part, this verse means the eastern.

The others keep the vision unresolved. Barnes fixes on what struck the seer as strange, that the destruction proceeded from the mouths rather than from trampling or sword or spear, and that power in the tail is natural language for a fish or a scorpion or a wasp but never for a horse; he insists the tails need be no more literal than the sulphur. Ellicott observes that the power is now in mouth and tail together where the earlier trumpet had the tail only, so that the devastation is increased, and he sets beside it the Chaldean cavalry of Habakkuk 1. He will offer the Turkish conquest and the unrestrained violence of revolutionary France as illustrations, but insists the teaching is the never-failing truth that worldliness provokes its own punishment. Robertson notes that the word for plague is the one used of Egypt, and ends by calling them surely dreadful monsters.
20:
What arrests every writer here is that the judgment fails of its purpose. Barnes puts it plainly: a third part is swept off, and it might reasonably have been expected that the remainder would be reformed and restrained, yet no reformation followed, no prevailing form of iniquity was abandoned, and the idolatry and superstition stood unchanged. He then declines to expound the two verses on the spot, holding that their meaning cannot be settled until the reference of the whole sixth trumpet is fixed, and he sets about fixing it. Robertson makes the same point out of the verb: the two-thirds still spared changed neither their creed nor their conduct.

Robertson also takes the list of idols as it stands. Both Testaments call the worship of images the worship of unclean spirits, which he thinks may be one explanation of the hideous faces given them; the enumeration by material — gold, silver, brass, stone, wood — he traces to the arraignment in Daniel 5:23, and the taunt that they can neither see nor hear nor walk to the psalms against idols. On the second verse he notes that murders heads the list, that the word rendered sorceries meant enchantment before it meant drug, and adds that our word pharmacy has come a long way out of a bad environment though a bad odour still clings to patent medicines.

Gill and Clarke both read the surviving two-thirds as the western church, spared by the Turks and unimproved by their neighbours' ruin. Gill names the countries the Turks did not reach and then the murders: the persecutions of the Waldenses and Albigenses, Huss and Jerome of Prague, the burnings under Queen Mary, the massacres in Paris and in Ireland, and the Inquisition, which continues still. Clarke's list is the same, with the crusades preached against the Albigenses, and he continues the identification through the other vices — the sorceries being the tricks and sleights of hand by which images of Christ are made to bleed and miracles pretended at tombs and holy wells, the fornication the honour given to creatures which is due only to the Creator, the thefts the exactions taken for indulgences and pardons.

Then Clarke turns and disowns the whole performance. These things may be intended, he writes, but it is going too far to say that this is the true interpretation; and yet to express any doubt on the subject is, with some, little else than heresy. If such men can see these things so clearly in prophecies so obscure, let them be thankful for their sight and indulgent to those who still sit in darkness. The rebuke is aimed at his own side, and it is the more pointed for standing at the end of an exposition he has just given in full.

Barnes meanwhile builds his case for the Turkish power from its appearance near the Euphrates to the taking of Constantinople in 1453, and the most interesting part of it is the numbering. Daubuz had suggested an allusion to the Turkman habit of reckoning by tomans, or myriads: Samarcand was rated at seven tomans because it could send out seventy thousand warriors, and the ancestors of Tamerlane were hereditary chiefs of a toman. Barnes observes that to no other invading host could the language be so well applied, and then says something that cuts against him as easily as for him — that if John were supposed to be writing after the event, this is the language he would have been likely to use, since it is nearly identical with the historian's. The uniform of red and blue and yellow he applies to the same hordes, allowing that it might fit other armies too, and asking only whether it fits these.
